case_study_insert.main_stem: Harborlight Bunkering (HBK) is a private limited company in the marine fuel bunkering sector, supplying low-sulphur fuel oil and LNG-blended bunker fuel to container ships and tankers calling at the harbour. Founded in 2013 by Lena Marchetti, it employs a workforce of 38 and operates a flat structure with autocratic leadership. HBK plans to invest $2,400,000 in a new LNG-fuelled bunker barge to serve the harbour's growing fleet, financed by a $1,500,000 seven-year bank loan and $900,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $280,000 a year, a variable cost of $42 a unit and a selling price of $50, and currently produces 55,000 units a year of marine fuel. HBK faces one operational problem: labour turnover among barge crew has reached 14% and is putting safety compliance at risk.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Quality and Safety Report — October 2026: HBK's bunker barge completed 1,240 fuel deliveries in the last 12 months at a near-miss rate of 0.9 per 1,000 tonnes, down from 1.7. Customer fuel over-delivery disputes fell from 9 to 3 per year. Average turnaround alongside customer ships is 2.6 hours. Market research of 150 shipping agents found that 72% would pay a 3% premium for certified LNG-blended bunkering and 66% require per-delivery emissions certificates for green corridor contracts. A training needs analysis shows 11 of 38 crew have not completed LNG bunkering certification; courses at the maritime college cost $1,100 per crew member. A training needs analysis found that crew need on-the-job training on LNG-blended fuel handling and off-the-job training for LNG certification before the blended-fuel rollout.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of Harborlight Bunkering for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) Global low-sulphur marine fuel prices have risen 18.6% year-on-year following refinery outages, raising bunker suppliers' procurement costs. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 7.1% from $12.90 to $13.82 per hour from April 2027, raising crew wage bills. (3) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 5.0% to 5.75%, increasing borrowing costs for vessel-owning businesses with variable-rate loans.

questions.question_text: HBK plans to fund part of the LNG-fuelled bunker barge with a $1,500,000 seven-year bank loan. Explain two advantages for HBK of using the bank loan to fund the expansion rather than draining its retained profit.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: A $1,500,000 bank loan spreads the cost of the new LNG-fuelled bunker barge over its working life, so HBK keeps its $900,000 retained profit as a liquid buffer. That buffer is vital when global low-sulphur fuel prices have risen 18.6% year-on-year and crew wages are about to rise 7.1% — HBK must fill its tanks and pay its 38 staff before the new barge earns a single dollar, and draining retained profit would leave no cushion if fuel prices climb further.

Point 2: Fixed seven-year loan repayments are predictable, which makes budgeting easier against a $280,000 fixed-cost base and helps HBK demonstrate solvency to the port authority and insurers when licensing the LNG barge. Keeping retained profit in the business also funds the $1,100 per crew member LNG certification and working-capital growth as volume builds toward and beyond 55,000 units a year, while the bank's involvement signals credibility to suppliers demanding prepayment.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to Harborlight Bunkering and its LNG bunker barge decision.

questions.question_text: HBK is launching LNG-blended bunkering for container ships calling at the harbour. Consider a full-page advertising campaign in a global shipping magazine, sponsorship of the international bunkering and ports conference, or a referral programme paying shipping agents commission on each delivery they route to HBK. Which should HBK choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Global shipping magazine advertising: A full-page campaign would present HBK's LNG-blended product, its 2.6-hour turnaround and its per-delivery emissions certificates to thousands of fleet managers worldwide. It builds prestige, but most readers never call at this harbour, the cost is high, and attention does not convert directly into booked fuel; for a 38-employee private limited company spending $2,400,000 on one barge, much of the spend would reach the wrong ports.

Sponsorship of the international bunkering and ports conference: Sponsorship puts HBK's name in front of buyers and regulators for two or three days, demonstrates its near-miss rate of 0.9 per 1,000 tonnes and its certification standards, and could win introductions to the exact 150 shipping agents it surveyed. However, it is expensive for a single event, results fade once the conference ends, and competitor LNG suppliers exhibit beside HBK, diluting the message.

Referral programme for shipping agents: The 150 agents surveyed shape which bunker supplier every vessel calls, and 72% said they would pay a 3% premium for certified LNG-blended bunkering while 66% want emissions certificates. Paying commission only on delivered tonnes ties cost directly to results, targets exactly the decision-makers with influence, and rewards agents with recurring, verifiable proof — ideal for a product with mandatory documentation.

Recommendation: HBK should choose the referral programme for shipping agents. It is the cheapest, most measurable and most targeted route to launch volume, it monetises the survey evidence that 72% of agents will pay a 3% premium, and it creates a durable sales channel into the harbour. The magazine campaign is rejected as too broad and slow to convert for one barge, and conference sponsorship is rejected as a costly one-off whose benefits decay; HBK should still attend the conference selectively using agent introductions the referral scheme generates.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited knowledge or outline of the promotion options with minimal context.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of the advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of HBK with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of HBK with a well-justified recommendation explaining why magazine advertising and conference sponsorship are rejected.

questions.question_text: HBK's labour turnover among barge crew has reached 14%. Explain two benefits for HBK of autocratic leadership for its barge crews.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Autocratic leadership gives barge crews one clear, immediate chain of command during bunkering, when a misunderstood instruction can cause a spill or a fire. HBK's near-miss rate of 0.9 per 1,000 tonnes is best protected by decisive orders from experienced masters rather than committee deliberation, keeping the 2.6-hour turnaround alongside customer ships and avoiding fuel over-delivery disputes recurring.

Point 2: With 11 of 38 crew still lacking LNG bunkering certification and labour turnover at 14%, fast induction and close supervision matter more than consultation. Autocratic leadership lets Lena Marchetti and her senior officers set exact safety routines for new and replacement crew, enforce them consistently on every delivery, and keep inexperienced staff compliant while the certification backlog clears — protecting the harbour licence and the business's safety record that customers pay the 3% premium for. Autocratic routine also keeps paperwork disciplined, so the 9-to-3 drop in over-delivery disputes is held and HBK's compliance file stays audit-ready for the LNG licence inspection.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to HBK's safety record, crew certification and turnover.

questions.question_text: HBK must certify 11 of its 38 crew on LNG bunkering. Consider on-the-job training mentored by senior barge officers or off-the-job training at the maritime college LNG bunkering course. Which should HBK choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
On-the-job training: Mentored training on HBK's own bunker barge teaches exactly the LNG coupling, venting and emergency shutdown procedures used on its hardware, costs nothing in fees, and keeps the 11 crew working through the 1,240 annual deliveries at a 2.6-hour turnaround. Drawbacks are that senior officers lose productive hours, unverified habits pass unchecked to new crew, and — critically — no portable, recognised certificate is produced, which shipping lines demanding per-delivery emissions paperwork and the port authority's LNG licence conditions may insist on.

Off-the-job training: The maritime college course at $1,100 per crew member gives all 11 crew structured simulator and classroom instruction leading to certified LNG bunkering competence, costing $12,100 in total — modest against a $2,400,000 barge. Crew are removed from rostered deliveries for the course duration, however, tightening scheduling during the launch, and generic content will not fully match HBK's specific barge systems, so a short on-site consolidation period would still be required.

Decision: HBK should choose the off-the-job maritime college course, followed by brief on-the-job consolidation. LNG handling is safety-critical and auditable; recognised certification is likely required by the port authority and requested by agents paying the 3% premium, and the $12,100 fee is trivial against the compliance and incident risk of uncertified fuel handling. Pure on-the-job training is rejected because it leaves HBK exposed on certification and safety verification exactly when fuel deliveries and vessel traffic are busiest, and because a single LNG incident would cost infinitely more than $12,100 in liability, lost licences and reputational damage with the port authority and the 150 shipping agents HBK depends on for routes.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two training methods with limited application to HBK.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of one or both training methods in the context of HBK.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both training methods in the context of HBK with a well-justified decision covering cost, safety, compliance and certification.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how HBK's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $280,000 ÷ ($50 − $42) = $280,000 ÷ $8 = 35,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 35,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $50 − $42 = $8.00. Answer: contribution per unit is $8.00.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways HBK's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. HBK's managers can compare the 35,000-unit break-even output with actual output of 55,000 units to confirm the bunkering operation is comfortably profitable, with a margin of safety of 20,000 units, informing whether to schedule extra LNG capacity or extend alongside times.
2. Contribution per unit of $8 lets HBK model discounts negotiated with shipping agents, for example a price cut to $47 would drop contribution to $5, letting managers judge whether the 3% green premium still leaves room to cover the $280,000 fixed costs.
3. Knowing fixed costs of $280,000 and contribution per unit helps managers stress-test repayments on the $1,500,000 bank loan for the new barge before launch, and to time the investment so the 55,000 units are covered before vessel calls peak.
4. Managers can use average total cost of $47.09 ($280,000 ÷ 55,000 + $42) to benchmark delivery economics quarter by quarter, flag procurement overspend against the 18.6% fuel-price rise, and decide whether to renegotiate supplier contracts before margin erodes.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 35,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $8.00 | (iii) Four contextual uses explained: margin of safety of 20,000 units vs 55,000-unit output; agent discount and 3% green premium modelling vs $280,000 fixed costs; loan-repayment feasibility for the $1,500,000 bank loan and $2,400,000 barge; and average total cost benchmarking at $47.09 to control procurement costs.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method, 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate HBK's financial performance by calculating the gross profit margin, profit margin and ROCE for 2024 and 2025. Has HBK's financial performance improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Gross Profit Margin 2024 = 35.0%
Gross Profit Margin 2025 = 40.0%
Profit Margin 2024 = 10.0%
Profit Margin 2025 = 12.0%
ROCE 2024 = 20.0%
ROCE 2025 = 22.5%

Detailed workings: 2024 revenue = $5,200,000 and gross profit = $1,820,000 against cost of sales of $3,380,000; 2025 revenue = $6,000,000 and gross profit = $2,400,000 against cost of sales of $3,600,000. 2024 operating profit = $520,000 against $5,200,000 of revenue (10.0%); 2025 operating profit = $720,000 against $6,000,000 of revenue (12.0%). 2024 capital employed = $2,600,000, 2025 = $3,200,000; interest payable rose from $118,000 to $140,000 after the larger borrowing. 2024 figure: $520,000 ÷ $2,600,000 = 20.0% on capital employed; 2025 figure: $720,000 ÷ $3,200,000 = 22.5%.

Evaluation: HBK's profitability has strengthened. Margins widened because revenue grew $800,000 while cost of sales grew only $220,000, reflecting firmer bunkering rates, the 3% green premium beginning to bite, and better procurement control despite the 18.6% fuel-price surge. Operating profit rose by $200,000, outpacing the $22,000 rise in interest payable, so the $1,500,000 loan is comfortably serviced. However, capital employed grew 23% from $2,600,000 to $3,200,000, meaning the business must keep converting scale into operating profit; a renewed fuel spike or agent-driven margin pressure could narrow the gains, and working capital tied up in fuel stocks deserves close watch.

Conclusion: HBK's financial performance has improved. Gross profit margin rose from 35.0% to 40.0%, the operating profit margin rose from 10.0% to 12.0%, and ROCE rose from 20.0% to 22.5%, leaving headroom to service the barge loan and fund LNG crew certification. The improvement is genuine but must be defended against fuel-price volatility before the new barge reaches full utilisation.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the gross profit margin, profit margin and ROCE for both 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratio calculations for both years combined with detailed evaluation of revenue, cost of sales, operating profit and capital employed movements and a justified conclusion on whether HBK's financial performance improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for HBK of introducing LNG-blended bunker fuel for its harbour fleet customers.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Certified LNG-blended bunkering lets HBK capture the 72% of 150 surveyed shipping agents willing to pay a 3% premium and satisfy the 66% demanding per-delivery emissions certificates for green corridor contracts. It differentiates HBK from conventional fuel-oil suppliers, wins higher-margin work from the busiest container lines, and strengthens the port's case to license the new LNG-fuelled bunker barge — lifting revenue beyond the current 55,000 units a year of low-sulphur fuel and giving HBK a premium product to bundle with emissions certificates when green corridor contracts are tendered, deepening switching costs against conventional suppliers.

Disadvantage: LNG bunkering demands $2,400,000 of new barge capacity, crew certified at $1,100 each and tighter safety and venting routines the autocratic crewing model must enforce without error. LNG supply also comes in fewer sources than fuel oil, so a single delayed cargo would stall the barge and idle 55,000 units of annual capacity; any incident involving uncertified crew would threaten the harbour licence and the 0.9 per 1,000 tonnes near-miss record customers rely on.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to HBK's research data, costs and safety record.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the 18.6% rise in marine fuel prices, the 7.1% minimum wage increase and the base interest rate rise to 5.75% will affect HBK. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Marine fuel price rise (18.6%): Fuel is the dominant component of HBK's $42 variable cost per unit. A 18.6% rise on a fuel component of, say, $30 adds roughly $5.60 per unit — about $308,000 a year at 55,000 units — and slashes contribution per unit from $8 toward $2.40 unless HBK reprices. HBK can pass some of this to agents through the 3% green premium and emissions-certificate pricing, but competitive pressure from rival bunker suppliers caps the pass-through; procurement hedging and tighter supplier contracts become essential.

Minimum wage increase (7.1%, to $13.82 per hour): With 38 crew and office staff, HBK's wage bill rises by roughly 7.1%. If average hourly pay is around $13.82, one full-time employee costs roughly $28,700 a year, so a 7.1% rise adds about $1,910 per worker — roughly $72,600 across the workforce. That is material against $280,000 fixed costs, and it arrives as the 11 uncertified crew are being trained and the 14% labour turnover is being tackled, squeezing HBK's ability to hold headcount steady during the launch.

Interest rate rise (5.0% to 5.75%): If the $1,500,000 seven-year bank loan is variable-rate, the 0.75% increase adds about $11,250 a year in interest. That is manageable and partly offsettable by holding profit before the LNG fleet ramps, and HBK could negotiate a fixed rate at renewal; the risk is small relative to fuel or payroll but does tighten cash while the barge is underperforming early volumes.

Conclusion: The 18.6% rise in marine fuel prices will have the greatest impact. It is by far the largest cash exposure, roughly $300,000 a year before mitigation, it directly compresses the $8 contribution that underpins the $2,400,000 barge investment, and it cannot be absorbed without repricing — whereas the wage rise is painful but absorbable through productivity, and the interest increase is the smallest in cash terms. HBK should respond with supplier hedging, premium invoicing to the 72% of agents willing to pay more, and strict fuel-stock controls before committing to the barge schedule.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external changes with limited application to HBK.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on HBK's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of HBK with a well-justified judgement that the marine fuel price rise has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.
